chapters.title: Nehemiah mourns and prays for Jerusalem

parts.text: While serving in the palace at Shushan, Nehemiah asks visitors from Judah about the returned Jews and Jerusalem. They report great affliction and disgrace: the city’s wall is broken and its gates burned. Nehemiah sits down and weeps, then mourns, fasts, and prays for several days.

He appeals to the God who keeps covenant and mercy, confessing Israel’s sins along with his own family’s failures. He recalls God’s warning of scattering for disobedience and promise of gathering those who return to him. Identifying Israel as God’s redeemed people, he asks for an attentive hearing and favor before the king, whom he serves as cupbearer.

chapters.title: Permission to rebuild and a night inspection

parts.text: Artaxerxes notices Nehemiah’s sadness. After praying, Nehemiah asks permission to rebuild Jerusalem, where his fathers are buried. The king grants leave, letters for safe passage, and timber, and sends an escort. Nehemiah attributes this favor to God’s good hand. Sanballat and Tobiah resent his arrival to seek Israel’s welfare.

After three days in Jerusalem, Nehemiah secretly inspects the ruined walls by night. He then tells the leaders what God and the king have done and calls them to rebuild. They agree and strengthen themselves for the work. When opponents mock them and accuse them of rebellion, Nehemiah expresses confidence that God will prosper his servants.

chapters.title: The people rebuild the wall together

parts.text: The chapter follows the rebuilding around Jerusalem, beginning with Eliashib and the priests at the sheep gate. Families, neighboring towns, rulers, goldsmiths, and other workers repair assigned sections and gates. Shallum works with his daughters. The Tekoites participate, though their nobles refuse to shoulder the work.

The record continues past the city of David, the priests’ houses, and the eastern gates until the circuit returns to the sheep gate. Some repair directly beside their own homes; others undertake additional sections. Levites, temple servants, merchants, and craftsmen contribute alongside officials. The names and locations show how many distinct groups share responsibility for restoring the city’s defenses.

chapters.title: Prayer, vigilance, and work under threat

parts.text: Sanballat and Tobiah mock the builders, but Nehemiah appeals to God and the people raise the wall to half its height. As the breaches close, surrounding enemies plan an attack. The builders pray and post guards, though exhaustion and repeated warnings increase their fear. Nehemiah stations families with weapons and urges them to remember the Lord and defend their households.

When the plot is exposed, work resumes with armed protection. Some stand guard while others labor, and builders keep swords beside them. A trumpet will summon scattered workers if danger comes. They work from dawn until the stars appear and remain within Jerusalem at night, combining continued construction with constant readiness.

chapters.title: Nehemiah confronts exploitation among the people

parts.text: Poor families cry out because famine, taxes, and debt have forced them to mortgage property and surrender children into bondage. Nehemiah rebukes the nobles and rulers for charging their brethren usury while others are trying to redeem Jews from foreign slavery. He demands restoration of property and the charges taken from them. The creditors agree under oath, and the people praise God.

Nehemiah recalls that during twelve years as governor he declined the usual allowance because the people were already heavily burdened. He and his servants worked on the wall rather than acquiring land, and he fed many at his own table. He asks God to remember his service for good.

chapters.title: Plots fail and the wall is completed

parts.text: With the wall nearly finished, Sanballat and Geshem repeatedly invite Nehemiah to a meeting intended to harm him. He refuses to abandon the work. An open letter then accuses him of planning rebellion and kingship. Nehemiah denies the invented charge and asks God to strengthen his hands.

Shemaiah urges him to hide in the temple from supposed assassins, but Nehemiah recognizes a hired attempt to make him sin and discredit him. The wall is completed in fifty-two days, and the enemies recognize God’s work. Yet Tobiah continues sending intimidating letters, supported by marriage connections and sworn loyalties among Judah’s nobles.

chapters.title: Jerusalem’s security and the register of returnees

parts.text: After completing the wall and setting its doors, Nehemiah appoints gatekeepers, singers, and Levites. Hanani and the faithful, God-fearing Hananiah receive charge of Jerusalem. Gate-opening rules and neighborhood watches protect the city, which remains sparsely populated. God moves Nehemiah to register the people by genealogy, and he finds the earlier returnees’ record.

That register lists families, towns, priests, Levites, and temple servants who returned with Zerubbabel. Some cannot prove their ancestry, and uncertain priestly claims remain restricted pending a decision. The congregation, servants, singers, and animals are counted. Gifts for the work are recorded, and the people’s settlement in their cities is noted.

chapters.title: The law is read and the feast restored

parts.text: The people gather before the water gate and ask Ezra to read Moses’ law. Men, women, and those able to understand listen attentively from morning until midday. The Levites explain the reading so the people understand it. When they weep, the leaders tell them the day is holy and call them to rejoice, share food, and find strength in the joy of the LORD.

Further study reveals the command to dwell in booths during the seventh-month feast. The people gather branches and make booths on roofs, in courts, and in public places. They celebrate with great gladness, hearing the law daily throughout the feast and keeping the concluding solemn assembly.

chapters.title: A confession of rebellion and repeated mercy

parts.text: Israel gathers with fasting and signs of mourning to read the law, confess sin, and worship. The Levites lead a prayer praising God as Creator and recalling his covenant with Abraham, deliverance from Egypt, law at Sinai, and provision in the wilderness. Despite the ancestors’ pride and the golden calf, God did not abandon them. He sustained them and gave their children the promised land.

The prayer recounts repeated rebellion, oppression, repentance, and merciful deliverance. Even after long resistance to the prophets, God preserved a remnant. The people acknowledge his justice and their own wrongdoing, describing their present servitude under foreign kings. In response, they make a written covenant sealed by their leaders.

chapters.title: The people pledge obedience and temple support

parts.text: The chapter names those sealing the covenant, including Nehemiah, priests, Levites, and family heads. The wider community joins them, with wives and children able to understand, binding themselves by oath to follow God’s law given through Moses and keep his commandments.

They promise not to intermarry with the surrounding peoples, buy goods on sabbaths or holy days, or neglect the seventh-year release. They undertake to provide money, wood, firstfruits, firstborn obligations, and tithes for worship and the support of priests and Levites. The Levites will bring a tithe of their tithes to the temple. Their commitment closes with a pledge not to forsake God’s house.

chapters.title: Families settle in Jerusalem and the towns

parts.text: Leaders already live in Jerusalem, and lots select one in ten of the remaining people to settle there. Those who offer willingly are blessed. The chapter lists families from Judah and Benjamin, along with priests, Levites, and gatekeepers, identifying their ancestry, numbers, and responsibilities in the holy city.

Others remain in their inherited towns, while temple servants live in Ophel. Duties for singers, officers, and those attending to royal affairs are noted. The closing section names settlements occupied by Judah and Benjamin, from southern towns to the villages around Jerusalem and beyond. Levites are distributed among both territories, supporting the restored community’s life outside the capital as well.

chapters.title: The wall is dedicated with thanksgiving

parts.text: The record names priests and Levites who returned with Zerubbabel and Jeshua and traces priestly succession through later generations. Heads of families, singers, and gatekeepers are identified, preserving the arrangements for thanksgiving and service associated with David’s commands.

For the wall’s dedication, Levites and singers gather from surrounding settlements. After purification, two great thanksgiving companies proceed along the wall and meet at the house of God, with music, trumpets, and sacrifices. Women and children share the rejoicing, which is heard far away. Officials are appointed over store chambers to receive and distribute the portions for priests, Levites, singers, and gatekeepers, maintaining the service the people gladly support.

Reading Moses’ law leads the people to separate the mixed multitude from Israel. Nehemiah recalls returning from the king to discover that Eliashib had given Tobiah a temple chamber. He throws out Tobiah’s goods and restores its sacred use. Finding that neglected support has driven Levites back to their fields, he restores their service and appoints faithful treasurers.

He stops sabbath trading, closes the gates, and warns persistent merchants. He also confronts marriages with foreign women, citing Solomon’s fall, and expels a priestly relative of Sanballat. He purifies the service, reassigns duties, and renews provision for wood and firstfruits. Throughout these reforms he asks God to remember him in mercy.
